role: Three compile-only candidates for the copy kernel. Not used in the 2026-11-17 rerun.
purpose: probe.c holds three candidate forms of the copy kernel `k_copy` of bandwidth.c, written only to compare their machine code. run_kernels.sh (the script of 2026-11-13) compiled the file without running it, and the rerun of 2026-11-17 does not use it.

main_flow.step: Nothing executes this file. It has no `main`, and run_kernels.sh compiles it to the object file probe.o without linking [Ref1].
Three macros define the parts of one loop pass: `LOADS` (16 loads, 256 B), `BARRIER` (the empty asm statement) and `STORES` (16 stores, 256 B).
Three functions build the copy loop from the macros: with the barrier, without it, and without both the barrier and `restrict`.
run_kernels.sh prints the machine code of each function into probe.txt. The reader compares the order of the loads and the stores there [Ref2].

behavior_notes: No function of this file runs in any test, and nothing here is timed. Among the scripts and the C sources of the project, only run_kernels.sh names the file: it compiles it and prints the machine code [Ref1].

The rerun of 2026-11-17 does not use this file. That rerun builds nothing. ra.sh uses the binaries bw_old and bw_new of 2026-11-13. None of the four scripts of the rerun (go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh, rx.sh) names this file [Ref4].
The file is about the copy kernel. It holds no read kernel. Its link to the read test is the macro `BARRIER`: the new read kernel `k_read` has the same empty asm statement after its 16 loads [Ref3].

Result of 2026-11-13 (gcc 14.2.0, flags `-O3 -march=native -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns -pthread -Wall -Wextra -std=gnu11`), per loop pass of 256 B: in candidate 1 all 8 `ldp` come before the 8 `stp`. Candidate 2 has 8 `ldp`, 7 `stp` and 2 `stur`, and loads and stores alternate. In candidate 3 all 8 `ldp` come before the 8 `stp` [Ref2].
The instruction sequence of candidate 1 equals that of `k_copy` in bw_new [Ref2].
Candidates 1 and 2 agree with the comment in bandwidth.c: with the empty asm statement the loads come first, without it loads and stores alternate [Ref3].
The results folder holds three runs of run_kernels.sh from 2026-11-13. Their three probe.txt files hold the same listing of these three functions [Ref2].
The probe.c in this folder has the sha256 value that probe.txt records for it (it starts with 81f96b39) [Ref2].

The bandwidth.c in this folder has the sha256 value that the run of 2026-11-13 18:32:18 UTC recorded for bandwidth.c (it starts with f1985072). The runs of 18:12:10 and 18:12:22 UTC recorded another sha256 value for bandwidth.c (c1406e02) [Ref2]. So the comment and the line numbers of bandwidth.c that this page cites are those of the later text. The binary bw_new had the same sha256 value in the three runs (it starts with fd7c14df), and the three probe.txt files hold the same listing of `k_copy` [Ref2]. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref5]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

words.def: an inner loop of the benchmark that reads, writes or copies memory. It never means the Linux kernel. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
`k_copy` of bandwidth.c: the loop that loads 256 B from a source buffer and stores them to a destination buffer in each loop pass.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
one of the three forms of the copy loop in this file.
C functions that map to Arm vector instructions. Here: `vld1q_u64` (load 16 B) and `vst1q_u64` (store 16 B).
the empty inline-assembly statement of the macro `BARRIER`.
a C keyword on a pointer. With it the programmer promises that no other pointer of the function reaches the same memory.
Arm instructions as they appear in the listing. `ldp` loads two 16-byte vector registers (32 B). `stp` stores two of them (32 B). `stur` stores one (16 B).
one unsigned 64-bit integer (8 bytes). The kernels take the buffer length as a count of words.
one run of the loop body of a kernel. Each kernel of bandwidth.c moves 256 B (32 words) per loop pass.
the output of the compiler for one source file, before linking. It cannot be run by itself.
the script of 2026-11-13. It built bw_old, bw_new and the self-test, compiled probe.c, printed the machine code of the kernels and ran the self-test. In its mode `all` it then timed the kernels.

a text file that run_kernels.sh wrote into its result folder. It holds the compiler, the flags, the sha256 values, the machine code of the kernels and the exit status of the self-test. During the rerun ra.sh writes another file with the same name into its own result folder. That file holds no machine code.
the tool that prints the machine code of a binary as text.
a checksum of a file. Two files with the same sha256 value have the same content.
the test under review: the 120-thread read test on CRB after the memory speed was lowered. Its scripts are go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh and rx.sh.
the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
